2018_119_032018regmtg.paragraph: Agenda packet for the Troy Board of Education regular meeting of March 20, 2018 at the Services Building — the meeting that both sold land and started building on it. The Board accepts Mondrian Properties' offer of $3,383,000.00 for 19.43 acres of surplus Section 16 land, splits 7.69 acres off the 80-acre Section 1 parcel for sale while committing the remainder to a conservation easement in perpetuity, authorizes up to $11,000,000 of 2018 School Building and Site Bonds without a vote of the electors to finance an early childhood center, and awards $17,963,193.15 of construction for that 72,000-square-foot preschool. It also awards $1,847,628.40 of network equipment to Presidio and $393,635.73 of musical instruments, vocal music and art supplies.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, March 20, 2018, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**Recognition**
The Mission Moment honors students and staff at Troy High, Athens, Boulan Park and Larson who reached out to Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida after the shooting the previous month — hundreds of letters and cards from Troy High and Boulan Park, student artwork from Athens, a banner from Larson's Craft Club. The Board also honors Larson Middle School as a **2018 State School of Character**, chosen on the implementation of 11 core principles, with its application forwarded for National School of Character consideration; Wass Elementary was named a 2018 Honorable Mention School of Character.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the February 6 workshop, the February 27 special workshop and the February 27 regular meeting, plus the January 2018 Treasurer's Report. At the February 27 special workshop, Boulan Park eighth grader Britta Pingree told the Board she was organizing the March 14 student-led walkout, to be held indoors, and asked the Board to keep promoting guns out of schools.

**Treasurer's Report — January 2018**
Total check disbursements are $6,656,519.98, of which the General Fund group is $4,995,284.07 and the General Fund (101) itself $4,677,126.87. With $3,084,461.32 of outgoing wire transfers, $127,829.82 of P-Card purchases and $45,814.58 of ACH debits, total disbursements in period are $9,899,747.70.

**Business 8.A — selling Section 16**
The district issued an RFP to purchase 19.43 +/- acres of surplus vacant land south of Long Lake, east of I-75 and west of Livernois (Sidwell 20-16-401-002) and received six proposals, examined with Clark Hill and consultant Great Northern. Rick West's March 15 memo tabulates the best-and-final offers:

| Purchaser | Price | Proposed project |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mondrian Properties | $3,333,000 or $50,000 above highest offer | 42 single family lots |
| GFA Development | $3,333,000 | 33 single family lots |
| JP Acquisitions, LLC | $3,240,000 | 33 single family lots |
| Clearview Homes | $3,171,000 | 35 single family lots |
| Pinnacle Homes | $2,975,000 | 35 single family lots |
| Robertson Homes | $2,310,000 to $2,520,000 | 33–39 single family lots |

Mondrian bid an escalator rather than a fixed number, and the resolution accepts its offer at a purchase price of **$3,383,000.00** with a $25,000.00 earnest money deposit.

**Business 8.B–8.D — dividing Section 1**
The 80 +/- acre Section 1 property (Sidwell 20-01-300-016 and 20-01-451-001) is split into a **7.69 +/- acre** parcel fronting Square Lake Road and a remainder Parent Parcel. The Board authorizes the lot split with the City of Troy's Assessor (8.B), then commits the remainder: maintained **in perpetuity in its natural and undeveloped condition**, except that the district may sell its wetlands mitigation credits to a third-party developer; a conservation easement negotiated with the MDEQ or a land conservancy; and, at closing, conveyance of the Parent Parcel to a conservancy along with **an estimated $150,000 of seed money** for its maintenance (8.C). Item 8.D authorizes an RFP for the 7.69-acre front parcel only, returning to the Board with a purchase agreement recommendation.

**Business 8.E–8.F — equipment**
Network equipment goes to **Presidio at $1,847,628.40** from the 2016 Capital Projects Fund. Four bids came in — CDW $2,215,578.22, Delta $1,835,891.19, Presidio $1,805,226.40 and Sentinel $2,946,971.40 — and Presidio is both lowest and compliant; the award adds Cisco ISE Endpoint Plus licensing ($14,976.00), outdoor access points at the two high schools and four middle schools ($23,602.00) and additional fiber ports at the Troy High MDF ($3,824.00).

Musical instruments, vocal music and art supplies are awarded across ten vendors totalling **$393,635.73** — Washington Music Center $186,732.40, Marshall Music $92,349.50, Dick Blick $29,979.00, Wenger $27,819.00, Evola Music $18,220.00, Music & Arts $15,423.20, Sam Ash $13,311.00, Woodwind & Brasswind $6,002.00, Lone Star Percussion $2,839.63 and K & S Music $960.00. Seventeen bidders were invited; twelve responded, two of them too late to be opened.

**Business 8.G — borrowing without a vote**
Having resolved in December 2017 to build an early childhood center, the Board authorizes **2018 School Building and Site Bonds (Limited Tax General Obligation) of not more than $11,000,000**. The authority is Section 1351(2) of Act 451, which lets a board issue bonds without a vote of the school electors so long as total outstanding bonded indebtedness is under 5% of the district's state equalized valuation. Final maturity is capped at 22 years; the bonds sell at public sale between 99% and 110% of par; PFM Financial Advisors LLC is financial advisor. PFM's presale runs a **3.57% NIC** on a 20-year structure at a 3.500% coupon, $11,000,000 of principal against $2,625,963 of interest on each side of the year for $16,251,925 of total principal and interest, with the required millage peaking at 0.20 mills.

**Business 8.H — building it**
Bid 9855 covers complete construction of a **72,000 square foot preschool building** in 19 separate bid categories, of which 3 — joint sealants, roller shades and casework — drew no acceptable bids and will be re-bid in fall 2018. Rob Carson recommends the low qualified bidder in each remaining category: total awards **$17,107,803.00** plus a 5% contingency of **$855,390.15**, for **$17,963,193.15** from the Early Childhood Center Fund. The largest packages are Titan Retail Industries general trades/exterior carpentry $3,204,000.00, Site Development sitework $2,535,000.00, Contrast Mechanical mechanical $1,658,000.00, City Contracting interior carpentry $1,348,800.00, Goyette electrical $1,324,287.00, Men of Steel $1,267,000.00 and Amalio Corporation concrete $1,017,600.00.

Agenda packet for the regular meeting of the Troy School District Board of Education, March 20, 2018, 7:00 PM at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. The agenda is: 1. Pledge of Allegiance; 2. Recognition — A. TSD Mission Moment: TSD Students Reach Out to Marjory Stoneman Douglas H.S. Students, B. State School of Character – Larson Middle School; 3. Additions & Deletions; 4. Public Communication (agenda items); 5. General – Consent Agenda; 6. Personnel; 7. Curriculum; 8. Business — A. Consideration: Section 16 Purchase Agreement, B. Consideration: Section 1 Property – Division of Parcel, C. Consideration: Section 1 Property – Preservation of Parent Parcel, D. Consideration: Section 1 Property – RFP Vacant Property (Front Parcel Only), E. Consideration: Wireless Networks and Switches, F. Consideration: Musical Instruments, Vocal Music and Art Supplies, G. Consideration: Early Childhood Financing, H. Consideration: Early Childhood Construction; 9. Public Communication (non-agenda items); 10. Other; 11. Adjournment. Meetings are cablecast on TS-TV Channel 19 (Comcast) and Channel 15 (WOW) every Monday and Wednesday at 2:00 and 9:00 p.m. when school is in session, and viewable at http://vimeo.com/troyschools.

**Recognition 2.A: outreach to Parkland students.** The Mission Moment honors students and staff at Troy High School, Athens High School, Boulan Park Middle School and Larson Middle School who took it upon themselves to reach out in a show of support to students at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, the scene of a deadly school shooting the previous month. At Troy High and Boulan Park, students, staff and teachers wrote hundreds of letters and cards to their counterparts in Florida, sending messages of love, prayers and positive thoughts. At Athens, students and art teachers sent student artwork and uplifting messages. At Larson, the Craft Club made a banner that could be hung at the school to let Stoneman Douglas students know that people as far away as Troy were thinking of them. The item observes that though there is no way to take away the pain students in Florida are feeling, the district is proud that its students and staff took the initiative to be part of the healing process. Certificates go to Boulan Park teachers Ann O'Neill and April Reem and student Britta Pingree; Larson teachers Amanda Fisher, Laura Garver and Katy Stanley; Athens teachers Jennifer McLellan and Melissa Velk; and Troy High teacher Jen Opalewski and students Emma Bossenberger, Quinn Kelly and Josiah Willis.

**Recognition 2.B: Larson Middle School, State School of Character.** A select few schools across the country are chosen each year as a State School of Character through the implementation of 11 core principles, which include promoting good character, culture and ethics; fostering student self-motivation; giving students the opportunity for moral action; and engaging families and community members as partners in character-building efforts. Larson was praised for the high quality of its work in all 11 principle areas, and its application has been forwarded for consideration as a National School of Character, to be announced later that spring. The item also commends Wass Elementary School, named a 2018 Honorable Mention School of Character and strongly encouraged to re-apply for the state designation the following fall. Larson Principal Joe Duda and teacher Charlie Tull receive the certificate.

**Consent agenda.** A. Minutes of the February 6, 2018 Board of Education Workshop; B. Minutes of the February 27, 2018 Special Board of Education Workshop; C. Minutes of the February 27, 2018 Board of Education Meeting; D. Treasurer's Report – January 2018.

The February 6 workshop, called to order by President Schmidt at 6:04 p.m. with Mrs. Hammond and Mr. Hauff absent, covered board professional learning — Diversity & Inclusion Part III with Dr. Jay Marks, Diversity Consultant from Oakland Schools, and a Technology Integration 4-Year Plan — a business services update on WAN fiber maintenance and the general trades package, a teaching and learning update on Schools of Choice 105 and 105c, the superintendent's update on enrollment projections, board committee assignments, and other items including the NSBA conference, the MASB Region 8 election, Five Dysfunctions of a Team next steps and a code of conduct update. It adjourned at 10:02 p.m.

The February 27 special workshop began at 6:34 p.m. with all seven members present, along with cub scouts from Wass Elementary, Troop 1708, and approximately 20 other members of the audience. In public communication, Britta Pingree, an eighth grade Boulan Park Middle School student, addressed the Board to share that she was organizing the March 14 student-led walkout at 10:00 a.m. related to the recent Parkland shooting. She indicated the walkout would be held indoors, encouraged students and the community to write letters to the families of the victims in Florida, and asked the Board to continue to promote keeping guns out of schools. The workshop adjourned at 6:58 p.m.

**The February 27, 2018 regular meeting minutes.** President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:02 p.m. with all seven members present — Fleming, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Miletti, Philippart and Schmidt — administrators Birmingham, Canfield, Cottone, Dziatczak, Jolly, Griffor, Harris and West, and approximately 150 members of the audience. Every resolution that evening carried 7-0.

The Board recognized the 2017-2018 senior scholar athletes, who maintained a 3.5 cumulative grade point average while participating in an athletic program, and the fall and winter All-State athletes. For the Mission Moment the Board honored Mr. David Easterbrook, benefactor of the new Auto Lab at Troy High. Troy High Principal Remo Roncone described Easterbrook's involvement: the owner of a Troy-based company providing facility design services and equipment to auto dealers across the country, he led the effort to engage outside help to develop a world-class instructional center. The new auto lab is the first phase in updating the high school's facilities to further enhance its STEM curriculum, with future plans for additional classes in automotive technology, engineering, robotics and the skilled trades. Resolution 18-016 adopted the Principal Appreciation Month resolution.

Resolution 18-017 approved the consent agenda. Dr. Machesky reported on enrollment projections, reviewing the district's history and the projections provided by Dr. Fred Ignatovich of Stanfred Consultants, explaining the data collected and analyzed for projecting enrollment for public school districts, the impact of Schools of Choice on current enrollment, the three projection scenarios — low, most likely and high — and how the projections are calculated, and comparing the projected 2017/2018 figures to the actual enrollment. Resolution 18-018 closed Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder and Boulan Park as well as Athens and Troy High to open enrollment for 2018-2019, with the exception of not more than 25 incoming ninth grade students residing in the Troy High attendance area who wish to attend Athens, and allowing students with siblings in grades 9 through 11 at Athens and Troy High to open enroll to remain.

Mark Dziatczak, Deputy Superintendent for Teaching & Learning, reported on the Schools of Choice recommendations, noting the factors weighed — current enrollment; enrollment projections, patterns and trends; numbers and percentages of Schools of Choice students currently in the district; the projected number of SOC siblings age-eligible to enter in 2018-2019; and available classroom space — and that the information had been reviewed in detail at the February 6 workshop. Resolutions 18-019 through 18-022 then adopted the four Schools of Choice resolutions: 40 nonresident kindergarten and 3 nonresident first grade students under Section 105 (within Oakland County) and again under Section 105c (outside Oakland County where the ISD is contiguous with Oakland ISD), and 14 total nonresident 6th-8th grade students at Baker, Larson and Smith Middle Schools under each of the two sections, with placement based on building availability.

Resolution 18-023 awarded fiber maintenance to Fiber Link, Inc. in the amount of $55,865.00 as an expenditure of the General Fund. Resolution 18-024 awarded bid pack 21A to R & E Development in the amount of $188,971.00 as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund. Resolution 18-025 adopted the 2018 Board Committee Memberships. Resolution 18-026 approved Mr. Gottlieb's attendance at the NSBA Annual Conference & Exposition in San Antonio, April 7-9, 2018. Resolution 18-027 cast the Board's MASB ballot for Mr. Donald Hubler of Macomb ISD.

Student representatives reported: Hana Barre (Troy High) on fundraisers for students in Flint following the water crisis and upcoming athletic events; Nadia Shaouni (Troy College & Career High School) on Spirit Week, reading to preschoolers in the TOTS program for March is Reading Month, and a Women of Tomorrow visit to the University of Michigan campus in April; Anjana Pisupati (International Academy-East) on Science Olympiad, the dance team and a Build On trip to Haiti; Tori Zarbaugh (Athens) was absent. In Board comments, Dr. Philippart congratulated the athletes and thanked Mr. Easterbrook, but noted there were no females in the video and asked how the district could help girls see this as a possible career; Mr. Gottlieb echoed her, recalling that he had only 7 female students in his class during his teaching career and wondering what should be done to open the program to more students; Dr. Machesky agreed more work is needed to make the program more viable in the future. Mr. Hauff remarked on the Wass scouts leading the Pledge of Allegiance and on Mr. Schmidt's pre-meeting overview to them of what a Board member's job entails, and announced the Athens Theatre Company's "Once Upon a Mattress." Mrs. Hammond described attending the K-2 Elementary Writers' Workshop at Leonard.

**Treasurer's Report, January 2018.** By the summary page, Total General Fund check disbursements are $4,995,284.07, with the General Fund (101) itself at $4,677,126.87, and TOTAL CHECK DISBURSEMENTS $6,656,519.98 — the same figure the check register carries as TOTAL REPORT 6,656,519.98. Adding ACH debits of $45,814.58, outgoing wire transfers of $3,084,461.32 and P-Card purchases of $127,829.82 gives TOTAL DISBURSEMENTS IN PERIOD $9,899,747.70. The middle sections of the packet are the January check register run by fund.

**Business 8.A: Section 16 purchase agreement.** The School District issued a Request For Proposals To Purchase Real Property to obtain proposals to purchase certain surplus vacant real property located in Section 16, and received six proposals, which the district examined in conjunction with its legal counsel, Clark Hill, and its consultant, Great Northern.

The resolution recites that the RFP covered 19.43 +/- acres of vacant land located south of Long Lake, east of I-75 and west of Livernois in Troy, Michigan, Sidwell Number 20-16-401-002; that the School District received an Offer To Purchase Real Estate from Mondrian Properties, an assumed name for Mondrian Properties, L.L.C., on behalf of an entity to be formed, to purchase the premises for a purchase price of Three Million Three Hundred Eighty Three Thousand and 00/100 ($3,383,000.00) Dollars with an earnest money deposit of Twenty Five Thousand and 00/100 ($25,000.00) Dollars; and that the district has reviewed the Offer and is desirous of accepting it. The resolution authorizes the sale on terms substantially similar to those in the attached Offer and authorizes the Superintendent, or his designee, to execute the Offer and any and all documents necessary and incidental to the sale.

Rick West's March 15, 2018 memorandum to the Board sets out the best and final offers received for the Section 16 property along with the projected number of homes from the six developers: Mondrian Properties at $3,333,000 or $50,000 above the highest offer, proposing 42 single family lots; GFA Development at $3,333,000 for 33 single family lots; JP Acquisitions, LLC at $3,240,000 for 33 single family lots; Clearview Homes at $3,171,000 for 35 single family lots; Pinnacle Homes at $2,975,000 for 35 single family lots; and Robertson Homes at $2,310,000 to $2,520,000 for 33 to 39 single family lots. Mondrian alone bid an escalator rather than a fixed figure, matching GFA's $3,333,000 and adding $50,000 over the highest competing offer; the purchase price carried into the resolution is $3,383,000.00. Copies of each proposal had been provided at the March 6 Board Workshop, and West recommends entering into a purchase agreement with Mondrian Properties as the high bidder. Mondrian also proposed the densest development of the six, 42 lots against 33 to 39 for the others.

**Business 8.B: Section 1 property, division of parcel.** The School District owns 80 +/- acres of vacant land commonly referred to as the Section 1 property, Sidwell Numbers 20-01-300-016 and 20-01-451-001. The resolution recites that the district desires to divide the premises into a parcel of 7.69 +/- acres containing frontage on Square Lake Road, with the balance to be known as the remainder of the Parent Parcel, and authorizes the Superintendent, or his designee, to apply for and obtain lot split approval from the City of Troy's Assessor and to obtain new sidwell numbers for the two individual parcels, together with any documents or surveys necessary and incidental to effectuate the split.

**Business 8.C: Section 1 property, preservation of the Parent Parcel.** Having authorized the split, the Board addresses what becomes of the land it keeps. Once lot split approval is obtained from the City of Troy, the Board authorizes the Superintendent or his designee to: maintain the remainder Parent Parcel in perpetuity in its natural and undeveloped condition, except that the School District shall have the authority to sell its wetlands mitigation credits to a third-party developer for reasonable consideration; negotiate the terms of and enter into a Conservation Easement with the Michigan Department of Environmental Quality or a land conservancy or other similar entity relative to the remainder Parent Parcel, on terms negotiated by the Superintendent or his designee and subject to review and approval by the district's legal counsel; and, simultaneously with the closing of the Conservation Easement, convey the remainder Parent Parcel to a land conservancy or other similar entity, including providing seed money for the maintenance of the conserved Parent Parcel estimated to be $150,000, again subject to counsel's review and approval. The operative resolution authorizes the Superintendent to negotiate and execute those agreements and any other documents necessary and incidental to conservation of the remainder Parent Parcel.

**Business 8.D: Section 1 property, RFP for the vacant front parcel only.** With the split authorized under 8.B and the remainder committed to conservation under 8.C, this resolution provides that once the district obtains lot split approval from the City of Troy, the Board authorizes the Superintendent or his designee to proceed toward the sale of the 7.69 +/- acre parcel fronting Square Lake Road through issuance of a Request for Proposal, returning to the Board with a recommendation for approval of a purchase agreement. Read as a set, items 8.A through 8.D dispose of two separate holdings on two different theories in one evening: Section 16 sold outright to a residential developer for $3,383,000.00, and Section 1 split so that only the 7.69 +/- acre road-frontage strip goes to market while the remainder Parent Parcel is placed permanently beyond development.

**Business 8.E: wireless networks and switches.** An RFP was issued to obtain competitive bids for upgrading the district's network equipment, reviewed by Beth Soggs, Director of Technology, and John Foster of Convergent Technology Partners. Foster's February 26, 2018 recommendation letter on Network Equipment Bid #9852 records that bids and proposals were received, opened and publicly read at 2:30 p.m. on January 23, 2018. Four proposals came in: CDW at $2,215,578.22, Delta at $1,835,891.19, Presidio at $1,805,226.40 and Sentinel at $2,946,971.40, with several voluntary alternates from Delta and Presidio. All bidders provided compliant proposals.

Foster recommends award to Presidio together with Voluntary Alternates #1, #3 and #5: base bid $1,805,226.40, Voluntary Alternate #1 at $14,976.00 for Cisco ISE Endpoint Plus licensing, Voluntary Alternate #3 at $23,602.00 for outdoor access points at Athens High, Troy High, Baker Middle, Boulan Park Middle, Larson Middle and Smith Middle, and Voluntary Alternate #5 at $3,824.00 for additional fiber ports at the Troy High MDF, for a total award of $1,847,628.40. Unlike the fiber maintenance award the month before, here the recommended vendor is also the low bidder: Presidio "has presented a solution that is both the lowest bid and meets the stringent requirements defined in the request for proposal," providing a highly reliable network with enough bandwidth to meet the district's needs for years to come. Listed features include dual-5GHz capability on access points offering nearly double the performance and capacity, automatic interference detection, classification and mitigation, a Cisco and Apple partnership offering access to Apple engineering, advanced RF tuning and optimization, automatic localization of wireless services such as AirPlay, AirPrint and Chromecast, and single-pane-of-glass management. The resolution awards the network equipment to Presidio in the amount of $1,847,628.40 as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.

**Business 8.F: musical instruments, vocal music and art supplies.** Invitations to bid were sent to seventeen potential bidders to provide closed sealed pricing for the required musical instruments, vocal music and art supplies. Twelve responses were received; two of those were not received prior to the due date and were not opened. Todd Hensley, Purchasing Supervisor, reviewed the proposals with Joe Havrilla, Instrumental Music Coordinator; Rosanne Thomas, Vocal Music Coordinator; and Katherine Hosbach, Visual Arts Coordinator, and they recommend the low bidders to specification.

The awards are: Dick Blick Company $29,979.00; Evola Music $18,220.00; K & S Music $960.00; Lone Star Percussion $2,839.63; Music & Arts $15,423.20; Marshall Music $92,349.50; Sam Ash Music $13,311.00; Washington Music Center $186,732.40; Wenger Corporation $27,819.00; and Woodwind & Brasswind, Inc. $6,002.00 — a total of $393,635.73, approved as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund. The packet carries the underlying line-item worksheets by building, itemizing instruments and equipment down to individual pieces such as a Wenger chair move and store cart for the Smith Middle School orchestra at $361.00.

**Business 8.G: Early Childhood financing.** In December 2017 the Board passed a resolution to proceed with the construction of an Early Childhood Center, and the district now proceeds with issuing general obligation school building and site bonds. The authority matters as much as the amount: Section 1351(2) of Act 451, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976, as amended, authorizes the board of education of a school district to borrow money and issue bonds or notes **without the vote of the school electors** if the total outstanding bonded indebtedness of the district is less than 5% of the state equalized valuation of the taxable property within the district. The Board deems it necessary to undertake the construction of an early childhood center facility, and deems it advisable to authorize bonds in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed Eleven Million Dollars ($11,000,000), or such lesser amount as determined by the Superintendent or Assistant Superintendent of Business Services, to pay a portion of the costs of the project and the costs of issuance. The district has posted notice under Section 308 of Act 34, Public Acts of Michigan, 2001, that the bonds will be secured by a pledge of the district's full faith and credit, subject to constitutional and statutory tax rate limitations, and must either be granted qualified status within the meaning of Act 34 or receive prior approval of the bonds from the Michigan Department of Treasury.

The attached authorizing resolution is captioned Troy School District, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, Resolution Authorizing 2018 School Building and Site Bonds (Limited Tax General Obligation), for a regular meeting held March 20, 2018 at 7:00 p.m. prevailing Eastern Time. It authorizes bonds designated the 2018 School Building and Site Bonds to be issued in one or more series in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $11,000,000. Bond details: registered as to principal and interest in denominations of $5,000 or integral multiples, dated as of the date of delivery or such other date as the Authorized Officer determines at sale, maturing May 1 or November 1 in principal amounts determined at sale, with **final maturity no later than twenty-two years from the date of issue**. The bonds shall be sold at public sale at a price not less than 99% and no more than 110% of principal amount, may be issued as serial or term bonds or both, and are subject to redemption prior to maturity at times and prices determined by the Authorized Officer; term bonds designated by the original purchaser are subject to mandatory redemption per the maturity schedule in the notice of sale. Interest is paid by check drawn on the Transfer Agent and mailed to the registered owner of record as of the fifteenth day of the month prior to each payment date; principal is payable at a bank or trust company selected as registrar and transfer agent; the bonds may be issued in book-entry-only form through The Depository Trust Company. The resolution appoints PFM Financial Advisors LLC as financial advisor and directs filings with the Municipal Advisory Council of Michigan at 535 Griswold, Suite 1850, with the Official Statement supplied under Rule 15c2-12.

PFM's presale schedule of estimated payments needed to retire the bonded debt models a 20-year, $11,000,000 issue at a **presale NIC of 3.57%**. The structure carries a 3.500% interest rate on all principal maturities, with no principal due in the first two years — interest only at $192,500 each side of the year — and principal beginning at $390,000 in tax year 2020 and rising to $750,000 in tax year 2039. Annual principal and interest sits close to $775,000 across the life of the issue, from $385,000 in the interest-only years up to a peak of $776,375. The totals are $2,625,963 of November 1 interest, $2,625,963 of May 1 interest, $11,000,000 of principal and $16,251,925 of total principal and interest. Projected taxable value grows from $3,747,756,940 in tax year 2017 at rates of 3.15%, then 1.00%, 1.50% and 2.00% thereafter, reaching $5,939,674,035 by tax year 2041, and the mills needed for all debt stay between 0.10 and 0.20 across the schedule.

**Business 8.H: Early Childhood Center construction.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on the construction of a new early childhood center, with responses reviewed by Rob Carson, Director of Operations, and the bond team of TMP Associates, Peter Basso & Associates and Barton Malow. Carson's March 14, 2018 memorandum to Rick West on RFP 9855 records that the scope of work included complete construction of a 72,000 square foot preschool building; that the RFP consists of 19 separate bid categories, 3 of which — joint sealants, roller shades and casework — will be re-bid in the fall of 2018 due to a lack of acceptable bids; and that all proposals were reviewed for bid thoroughness, accuracy and project alternates by the project team of Barton Malow, TMP and Lecole Planners. He recommends the low qualified bidder in each remaining category.

The awards are: 03000 Concrete, Amalio Corporation, $1,017,600.00; 04000 Masonry, Baker Construction, $830,300.00; 05000 Steel, Men of Steel, $1,267,000.00; 06000 General Trades/Exterior Carpentry, Titan Retail Industries, $3,204,000.00; 07000 Roofing/Shingles, Streng Roofing, $742,000.00; 08000 Exterior Doors/Aluminum Windows, Hewett Company, $490,000.00; 09200 Interior Carpentry, City Contracting, $1,348,800.00; 09300 Tile, Empire Tile, $178,550.00; 09650 Flooring, Conventional Carpet, $389,000.00; 09900 Painting, Continental Contracting, $53,500.00; 10110 Visual Display, Cig-Jan Products, $44,377.00; 11400 Food Service Equipment, Stafford-Smith Co., $119,919.00; 21100 Fire Suppression, Professional Sprinkler, $199,780.00; 22000 Plumbing, Contrast Mechanical, $940,000.00; 23000 Mechanical, Contrast Mechanical, $1,658,000.00; 23093 Temperature Controls, MCMI, Inc., $433,000.00; 26000 Electrical, Goyette Company, $1,324,287.00; 32000 Sitework, Site Development, $2,535,000.00; and 32120 Paving, Nagle Paving, $332,690.00. Total awards are $17,107,803.00, the 5% contingency is $855,390.15, and the total recommended amount is $17,963,193.15. A separate purchase order will be issued for each bid category, funded from the ECC Fund. The resolution awards bid 9855 in the amount of $17,963,193.15 as an expenditure of the Early Childhood Center Fund.

The attached bid tabulation records the allowances included in the base bids and removed during post-bid reviews — $20,000 general trades, $50,000 interior carpentry, $100,000 mechanical (Barnard, Bemis, Wass Addendum #1) and $30,000 electrical — with the $120,000 sitework allowance kept. It also shows how close the concrete category was: Amalio at $1,010,800.00 with a bid clarification adding exterior column enclosures at $6,800.00, against McCarthy Construction at $1,025,200.00, Gemelli Concrete at $1,169,000.00 and Fessler Bowman at $1,260,000.00, with each bidder's familial-disclosure and Iran-certification boxes checked.

Taken as a whole, this is the meeting at which the Early Childhood Center stopped being a decision and became a project: an $11,000,000 borrowing authorized without going to the voters under the Act 451 debt-capacity test, and $17,963,193.15 of construction awarded the same evening — the gap between the two covered from the district's own Early Childhood Center Fund and, in part, by the proceeds of the land it was selling in the four business items immediately preceding.
